newsitem.title: UK: Food aid deal for the world's poorest awaits WTO.
newsitem.headline: Food aid deal for the world's poorest awaits WTO.

text.p: Poor nations can expect that donors will revamp procedures for food aid during 1997 under pressure of Uruguay Round free trade rules, diplomats and food officials said.

A World Food Convention is overseen by the London-based International Grains Council (IGC), a group of leading exporting and consuming nations, and delegates held talks on its future in London this week. At present, it commits food-rich countries to a minimum food aid shipment of 5.4 million tonnes of wheat equivalent to the least developed countries every year.
But the convention expires in June 1998 and donors are timing negotiations on a future accord to take account of the outcome of a WTO ministerial meeting in Singapore next week.
"The members are aware that we will need to look at the convention again next year in order for something to happen by June 1998," said one Western diplomat.
"Members' views will be partly influenced by anything that comes out of Singapore."
The WTO will meet between December 8-13 and bring together the 125 current WTO members and several others on the waiting list to join.
The agenda will have little room for agriculture.

But delegates are expected to sign an annex drafted by the WTO agriculture committee on steps to counter negative impacts on poor food importing countries from the Uruguay Round of free trade measures.
The annex makes provision for additional food aid shipments or financial and technical assistance for poor nations if trade liberalisation has harmful effects on their food security.

Diplomats said, however, that the measures were vaguely defined and implied little more than just a statement of intentions regarding future policies on food aid. Donor countries have so far exceeded minimum requirements each year. For instance, shipments in 1996/97 (July/June) are forecast to reach seven million tonnes or 1.6 million above the minimum.
Pressures on poor nations' food import bills have also eased lately as world prices have dropped from historic highs following bumper harvests around the globe this year.
But spearheaded by moves by the United States to trim spending, minimum food aid obligations were cut two years ago and importers remain vulnerable to any new "spike" in prices.

"The concern is that they have to be compensated one way or another for the expected higher food price in the future," said Werner A. Lamade, head of the commodities and trade division of the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
"But the question is how will it be implemented? How will more food or financial aid be given?".

Participants in the Food Aid Convention look to a prospect of organising meetings after the Singapore WTO session. No date has been set but talks are expected to start next year to allow time for parliaments to endorse decisions.
"Steps will be taken next year to look at what scope there is among current donors to either renew or roll over the convention," said the Western diplomat.
